items.context:
Pōhutukawa (New Zealand Christmas tree), Metrosideros excelsa, is found only in New Zealand. Broad, spreading coastal tree, often on cliffs, with a gnarled trunk and hanging aerial roots. Leaves are thick and leathery with dense white felt underneath, and young shoots and buds are woolly. Masses of crimson brush-like flowers (bunches of long stamens) from late November to January; small woody seed capsules follow.

In this photo: Wide, umbrella-shaped evergreen crown on a gnarled, multi-stemmed trunk growing on a coastal cliff edge; dense grey-green foliage.

Photo: Bjankuloski06 (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Broad, spreading coastal tree, often on cliffs, with a gnarled trunk and hanging aerial roots. Leaves are thick and leathery with dense white felt underneath, and young shoots and buds are woolly.

media.alt: A broad, dome-crowned tree with twisting branches leaning out over a grassy clifftop above the sea

items.context:
Rātā (northern rātā), Metrosideros robusta, is found only in New Zealand. Huge forest tree that usually starts life as an epiphyte high on another tree, sending roots down that fuse into a massive, fluted, hollow trunk. Flowers look like pōhutukawa but the leaves are smaller, glossy and lack white felt underneath. Scarlet brush flowers in summer (mostly December–January), with heavy flowering in some years and sparse flowering in others.

In this photo: Emergent tree with dense dark-red flowering crown towering over mixed lowland forest.

Photo: John Barkla (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Huge forest tree that usually starts life as an epiphyte high on another tree, sending roots down that fuse into a massive, fluted, hollow trunk. Flowers look like pōhutukawa but the leaves are smaller, glossy and lack white felt underneath.

media.alt: A large tree with a rust-red flowering crown rising above surrounding forest on a hillside

items.context:
Kōwhai, Sophora microphylla, is found only in New Zealand. Small tree with feathery leaves made of many tiny paired leaflets, and drooping clusters of golden tubular flowers in late winter to spring. Several kōwhai species look alike; this one has a tangled, zigzag juvenile stage. Golden-yellow pea flowers (often before or with new leaves) from about August to October, followed by knobbly, beaded seed pods with hard yellow seeds.

In this photo: Adult tree form: single trunk with open, spreading crown; crown turned gold by hanging yellow flowers in early spring, when many leaves have fallen.

Photo: John Barkla (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Small tree with feathery leaves made of many tiny paired leaflets, and drooping clusters of golden tubular flowers in late winter to spring. Several kōwhai species look alike; this one has a tangled, zigzag juvenile stage.

media.alt: A small tree on a grassy bank with a sparse crown tinged golden-yellow by flowers

items.context:
Harakeke (New Zealand flax), Phormium tenax, is found only in New Zealand. Large clump of stiff, tough, sword-shaped leaves up to 3 m long that fan from the base. Tall dark flower stalks rise well above the leaves; seed pods are short, stiff and point upward. Dull red tubular flowers on stalks up to 4–5 m from October to December, much visited by tūī; upright three-sided pods follow.

In this photo: Big fans of tough, keeled, strap-like leaves up to 2–3 m long, held stiffly upright with only the tips bending.

Photo: Dawn Hendrikse (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Large clump of stiff, tough, sword-shaped leaves up to 3 m long that fan from the base. Tall dark flower stalks rise well above the leaves; seed pods are short, stiff and point upward.

media.alt: Large clumps of long, stiff, upright sword-shaped leaves at the edge of a grassy area

items.context:
Wharariki (mountain flax), Phormium cookianum, is found only in New Zealand. A smaller, softer flax than harakeke with thinner leaves that arch and droop. The surest cue is the seed pods: long, slender, twisted and hanging down. Greenish-yellow flowers in early summer, then long twisted pods that dangle from the flower stalk.

In this photo: Flax-like fan of strap leaves that are thinner and floppier than harakeke, arching over at the ends.

Photo: Krzysztof Golik (CC BY-SA 4.0).

practices.explanation: A smaller, softer flax than harakeke with thinner leaves that arch and droop. The surest cue is the seed pods: long, slender, twisted and hanging down.

media.alt: A dense clump of long, narrow, arching grey-green leaves in coastal scrub

items.context:
Tī kōuka (cabbage tree), Cordyline australis, is found only in New Zealand. Tree with a bare corky trunk that forks into branches, each ending in a dense pom-pom of long, narrow, grass-like leaves. Dead leaves hang as a skirt beneath each tuft. Huge sprays of tiny, sweet-scented creamy flowers in late spring (October–December), then small bluish-white berries.

In this photo: Branched trunk ending in round pom-pom heads of long, narrow, grass-like leaves; dead leaves hang as a skirt below each tuft.

Photo: larivera (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Tree with a bare corky trunk that forks into branches, each ending in a dense pom-pom of long, narrow, grass-like leaves. Dead leaves hang as a skirt beneath each tuft.

media.alt: A tree with a bare trunk dividing into several branches, each topped by a dense tuft of long narrow leaves

items.context:
Ponga (silver fern), Alsophila dealbata, is found only in New Zealand. Tree fern whose mature fronds are bright silvery-white underneath. Old frond bases stay on the trunk as stubs rather than a full skirt of dead fronds. No flowers (spore-producing).

In this photo: Slender trunk topped by a flat crown of arching fronds; old dead stalk bases on trunk rather than a hanging skirt.

Photo: Ashley M Bradford (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Tree fern whose mature fronds are bright silvery-white underneath. Old frond bases stay on the trunk as stubs rather than a full skirt of dead fronds.

media.alt: A tree fern with a slender dark trunk and a spreading crown of fronds beside a forest path
media.credit: Photo: Ashley M Bradford, CC BY-NC 4.0, https://www.inaturalist.org/photos/60161927

items.context:
Mamaku (black tree fern), Sphaeropteris medullaris, is native to New Zealand. New Zealand's tallest tree fern, with very long arching fronds on thick black stalks. Old fronds drop off cleanly, leaving a trunk patterned with oval or hexagonal scars, and the young koru are covered in black scales. No flowers (spore-producing).

In this photo: Very large tree fern whose frond stalks are thick, black and arching; old fronds fall off cleanly leaving a trunk patterned with oval scars.

Photo: Duncan Cunningham (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: New Zealand's tallest tree fern, with very long arching fronds on thick black stalks. Old fronds drop off cleanly, leaving a trunk patterned with oval or hexagonal scars, and the young koru are covered in black scales.

media.alt: A tree fern seen from below, with thick black frond stalks radiating from the top of the trunk

items.context:
Wheki (rough tree fern), Dicksonia squarrosa, is found only in New Zealand. Slender, dark tree fern whose trunk bristles with the snapped-off bases of old frond stalks. Frond stalks are rough with dark brown hairs, and fronds are green on both sides; it often grows in clumps. No flowers (spore-producing).

In this photo: Thin dark trunk studded with the snapped-off bases of old frond stalks; dead fronds hang untidily but do not form a full skirt.

Photo: catchwords (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Slender, dark tree fern whose trunk bristles with the snapped-off bases of old frond stalks. Frond stalks are rough with dark brown hairs, and fronds are green on both sides; it often grows in clumps.

media.alt: A slender tree fern with a dark, rough trunk and a crown of fronds, some dead and brown, in regenerating bush

items.context:
Nīkau (nīkau palm), Rhopalostylis sapida, is found only in New Zealand. New Zealand's only native palm: a slender ringed grey trunk, a smooth bulging green crownshaft, and stiff, upswept feather-like fronds like a feather duster. Pinkish-lilac branched flower clusters burst from just below the crownshaft (summer–autumn), followed by slowly ripening bright red berries.

In this photo: Only native palm: slender grey trunk with leaf-scar rings, a swollen green crownshaft below stiff, upward-angled feather-shaped fronds.

Photo: waynemitchell (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: New Zealand's only native palm: a slender ringed grey trunk, a smooth bulging green crownshaft, and stiff, upswept feather-like fronds like a feather duster.

media.alt: A tree with a slender ringed trunk, a smooth bulging green shaft and a stiff, upswept crown of feather-like fronds

items.context:
Kauri, Agathis australis, is found only in New Zealand. Giant conifer of northern forests with a massive, straight, branchless trunk of smooth grey bark that flakes in thick round scales, crowned high above the canopy. Leaves are thick, leathery and strap-shaped; cones are round balls. Round female cones (spring to autumn) break apart on the tree to release winged seeds; small cylindrical male cones occur on the same tree.

In this photo: Mature tree: enormous, column-like, branchless trunk with smooth grey flaking bark; the crown sits high above the rest of the forest.

Photo: Leon Perrie (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Giant conifer of northern forests with a massive, straight, branchless trunk of smooth grey bark that flakes in thick round scales, crowned high above the canopy. Leaves are thick, leathery and strap-shaped; cones are round balls.

media.alt: A colossal straight grey trunk rising without branches beside a forest boardwalk

items.context:
Rimu (red pine), Dacrydium cupressinum, is found only in New Zealand. Tall forest conifer whose branchlets hang down in soft, drooping ropes of tiny, overlapping, scale-like needles. Bark peels in large, thick flakes. Small fruits: a black seed on a red fleshy cup, mostly February–May, and heavily only in mast years.

In this photo: Mature tree: tall emergent with a long clean trunk and a crown of drooping branchlets gathered in clumps.

Photo: Christopher Stephens (CC BY-SA 4.0).

practices.explanation: Tall forest conifer whose branchlets hang down in soft, drooping ropes of tiny, overlapping, scale-like needles. Bark peels in large, thick flakes.

media.alt: A tall tree with a straight bare trunk and clumped, rounded crown standing above surrounding forest

items.context:
Tōtara, Podocarpus totara, is found only in New Zealand. Large conifer with thick, reddish-brown, stringy bark that peels in long strips. Leaves are stiff, leathery, brownish-green and end in a sharp prickly point. Pollen cones appear in spring; fruits (a seed on a swollen red fleshy base) ripen mostly in autumn.

In this photo: Very thick trunk with reddish-brown, stringy bark peeling in long strips; dense dark green crown.

Photo: Colin Meurk (CC BY-SA 4.0).

practices.explanation: Large conifer with thick, reddish-brown, stringy bark that peels in long strips. Leaves are stiff, leathery, brownish-green and end in a sharp prickly point.

media.alt: A massive old tree with a thick, fluted, stringy-barked trunk and a dense dark crown

items.context:
Kahikatea (white pine), Dacrycarpus dacrydioides, is found only in New Zealand. New Zealand's tallest tree, a slender conifer with a narrow crown, typical of swamps and wet river flats (often left standing in paddocks). Trunk bases are buttressed and adult foliage is tiny, overlapping scales. Fruits ripen February–April: a blue-black seed sitting on a swollen orange-red fleshy base.

In this photo: Very tall, slender tree with a narrow, tapering crown, often left standing in wet paddocks; NZ's tallest native tree.

Photo: Krzysztof Golik (CC BY-SA 4.0).

practices.explanation: New Zealand's tallest tree, a slender conifer with a narrow crown, typical of swamps and wet river flats (often left standing in paddocks). Trunk bases are buttressed and adult foliage is tiny, overlapping scales.

media.alt: A tall, narrow, solitary conifer with a slim crown standing in flat farmland

items.context:
Mataī (black pine), Prumnopitys taxifolia, is found only in New Zealand. Conifer with dark grey bark that falls away in thick round flakes, leaving reddish 'hammer-mark' scars. Adult leaves are short, flat, blunt needles in two rows, pale bluish underneath. Round, dark blue-black to plum-coloured fruits about 1 cm across with a waxy bloom; they take 12–18 months to ripen.

In this photo: Straight trunk with dark bark falling away in thick, rounded flakes; crown of small, dark foliage high up.

Photo: Jaz Morris (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Conifer with dark grey bark that falls away in thick round flakes, leaving reddish 'hammer-mark' scars. Adult leaves are short, flat, blunt needles in two rows, pale bluish underneath.

media.alt: Looking up a straight, tall trunk covered in dark scaly bark to a high crown

items.context:
Miro (brown pine), Pectinopitys ferruginea, is found only in New Zealand. Conifer with feathery sprays of flat, slightly curved needles in two rows, bright to bronze-green. Its plum-like pink-red fruits are unlike any other native conifer. Pink-red, waxy, plum-shaped fruits (about 2 cm) mostly November–April; a favourite food of kererū.

In this photo: Glossy pink-red to purple, plum-shaped fleshy fruits (2 cm) dangling on short stalks; much loved by kererū.

Photo: greghadley1 (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Conifer with feathery sprays of flat, slightly curved needles in two rows, bright to bronze-green. Its plum-like pink-red fruits are unlike any other native conifer.

media.alt: Several plum-like pinkish-red fruits with a waxy bloom hanging among flat, curved needles

items.context:
Mānuka (tea tree), Leptospermum scoparium, is native to New Zealand. Shrub or small tree with small, stiff, sharp-pointed leaves that prick when you squeeze a twig. Flowers are relatively large and borne singly; hard woody seed capsules stay on the stems for years. White (sometimes pink) five-petalled flowers about 1–1.5 cm across, mainly spring to summer.

In this photo: Wiry, upright shrub covered in white five-petalled flowers set singly along the stems; tiny dark leaves.

Photo: Peter de Lange (pjd1) (CC0 1.0).

practices.explanation: Shrub or small tree with small, stiff, sharp-pointed leaves that prick when you squeeze a twig. Flowers are relatively large and borne singly; hard woody seed capsules stay on the stems for years.

media.alt: An upright shrub with thin stems densely dotted with small white flowers among rough grass

items.context:
Kānuka (white tea tree), Kunzea robusta, is found only in New Zealand. Small tree, often with several slender trunks and long strips of loose papery bark. Leaves are soft and not prickly, and the small flowers come in dense, fluffy masses. Small white flowers (under 1 cm) crowded along the twigs, giving trees a snowy look in late spring and summer; tiny capsules fall soon after ripening.

In this photo: Small trees with many slim trunks and long strips of loose, papery grey-brown bark; fine, feathery canopy.

Photo: Bjankuloski06 (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Small tree, often with several slender trunks and long strips of loose papery bark. Leaves are soft and not prickly, and the small flowers come in dense, fluffy masses.

media.alt: A sandy track through a stand of small trees with slender, leaning, shaggy-barked trunks

items.context:
Karaka (New Zealand laurel), Corynocarpus laevigatus, is found only in New Zealand. Medium tree with a dense, dark canopy of large, thick, very glossy leaves. Bunches of oval fruits ripen bright orange; the kernels are poisonous unless specially treated. Small greenish flowers in spring; orange plum-sized fruits January–April.

In this photo: Dense, dark green, very glossy canopy on a medium tree with smooth pale trunks.

Photo: Shaun Lee (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Medium tree with a dense, dark canopy of large, thick, very glossy leaves. Bunches of oval fruits ripen bright orange; the kernels are poisonous unless specially treated.

media.alt: A tree with a dense, dark, glossy rounded crown on several pale trunks beside a car park

items.context:
Pūriri, Vitex lucens, is found only in New Zealand. Spreading northern tree with glossy, wavy leaves divided into 3–5 leaflets that radiate from one point. Pink tubular flowers and red cherry-like berries appear for much of the year, and trunks often show holes made by pūriri moth larvae. Bright pink-red, two-lipped flowers mostly in winter and spring, with red berries present most of the year.

In this photo: Large, gnarled trunk with spreading branches; often hollowed with holes from pūriri moth larvae.

Photo: Jacqui Geux (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Spreading northern tree with glossy, wavy leaves divided into 3–5 leaflets that radiate from one point. Pink tubular flowers and red cherry-like berries appear for much of the year, and trunks often show holes made by pūriri moth larvae.

media.alt: An old tree with a massive, twisted, leaning trunk and spreading limbs over a bush track

items.context:
Rewarewa (New Zealand honeysuckle), Knightia excelsa, is found only in New Zealand. Tall, narrow, column-shaped tree that stands out above regenerating bush. Leaves are long, stiff, leathery and bluntly toothed; new growth and buds are covered in rusty-brown fuzz. Dark red, bottlebrush-like flower clusters with curled petals on older wood, October–December; velvety brown seed pods follow.

In this photo: Distinctive slender, upright, poplar-like shape with a narrow crown and dark foliage.

Photo: Rudolph89 (CC BY-SA 3.0).

practices.explanation: Tall, narrow, column-shaped tree that stands out above regenerating bush. Leaves are long, stiff, leathery and bluntly toothed; new growth and buds are covered in rusty-brown fuzz.

media.alt: A tall, narrow, column-shaped tree with dark foliage standing in a park

items.context:
Kawakawa (pepper tree), Piper excelsum, is found only in New Zealand. Shrub with jointed, knobbly stems and broad heart-shaped leaves with veins fanning from the base, usually peppered with holes from looper caterpillars. Crushed leaves smell peppery. Upright candle-like flower spikes in spring; on female plants they swell and ripen to orange.

In this photo: Bushy shrub with jointed, knobbly stems and many broad heart-shaped leaves, often riddled with holes chewed by looper caterpillars.

Photo: Jenny Christianson (kaipatiki_naturewatch) (CC0 1.0).

practices.explanation: Shrub with jointed, knobbly stems and broad heart-shaped leaves with veins fanning from the base, usually peppered with holes from looper caterpillars. Crushed leaves smell peppery.

media.alt: A dense shrub of broad, rounded, heart-shaped leaves beside a bush track

items.context:
Horopito (red horopito), Pseudowintera colorata, is found only in New Zealand. Small shrub with oval, leathery, yellow-green leaves blotched and edged with red, and pale bluish-white undersides. The leaves taste hot and peppery. Small greenish-yellow flowers in summer, then red to black berries.

In this photo: Small bushy shrub of the forest edge with yellowish-green leaves splashed and edged with red.

Photo: Mike Dickison (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Small shrub with oval, leathery, yellow-green leaves blotched and edged with red, and pale bluish-white undersides. The leaves taste hot and peppery.

media.alt: A low leafy shrub with yellow-green leaves blotched with red growing beside a forest track

items.context:
Horoeka (lancewood), Pseudopanax crassifolius, is found only in New Zealand. Tree that changes dramatically with age. Young plants carry very long, rigid, narrow, toothed leaves pointing down; adults become a tall bare trunk with a small rounded crown of shorter leaves. Small greenish flowers in late summer, then purplish-black fruit.

In this photo: Juvenile: unbranched stem with very long (up to 1 m), rigid, narrow, toothed leaves all pointing down.

Photo: tomasblokker (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Tree that changes dramatically with age. Young plants carry very long, rigid, narrow, toothed leaves pointing down; adults become a tall bare trunk with a small rounded crown of shorter leaves.

media.alt: A single slender stem with long, stiff, narrow leaves angled steeply downward like a half-closed umbrella

Koromiko (hebe), Veronica stricta, is found only in New Zealand. Fast-growing shrub of open ground and forest edges with long, narrow, bright green leaves in opposite pairs. Long, tapering spikes of small white to pale lilac flowers stick out among the leaves. Flower spikes mainly late winter to spring, but some can appear at any time of year.

In this photo: Rounded shrub with long (5–15 cm), narrow, willow-like leaves in opposite pairs and long, tapering spikes of white to pale lilac flowers.

Photo: Kate McAlpine (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Fast-growing shrub of open ground and forest edges with long, narrow, bright green leaves in opposite pairs. Long, tapering spikes of small white to pale lilac flowers stick out among the leaves.

media.alt: A leafy shrub of long, narrow, bright green leaves with slender white flower spikes poking out

items.context:
Kōhūhū (black matipo), Pittosporum tenuifolium, is found only in New Zealand. Small tree with small, wavy-edged, glossy light-green leaves on almost black twigs. Tiny, dark purple-red flowers smell of honey in the evening. Dark red to almost black flowers in spring (October–November); black-seeded capsules in late summer.

In this photo: Compact, upright small tree with dense fine foliage on slender dark stems.

Photo: Tom Beard (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Small tree with small, wavy-edged, glossy light-green leaves on almost black twigs. Tiny, dark purple-red flowers smell of honey in the evening.

media.alt: A small upright tree with a dense, rounded crown of small pale green leaves

items.context:
Tarata (lemonwood), Pittosporum eugenioides, is found only in New Zealand. Small tree with pale yellow-green, glossy leaves that have very wavy edges and a pale midrib; crushed leaves smell of lemon. Bark is pale grey. Clusters of small, pale yellow, sweet-scented flowers at the branch tips, October–December.

In this photo: Small tree with a dense crown of noticeably light, yellowish-green foliage and pale grey bark.

Photo: Heidi Meudt (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Small tree with pale yellow-green, glossy leaves that have very wavy edges and a pale midrib; crushed leaves smell of lemon. Bark is pale grey.

media.alt: A dense, bushy small tree with pale yellow-green foliage

items.context:
Karamū, Coprosma robusta, is found only in New Zealand. Large shrub or small tree with glossy, opposite, oblong leaves 6–12 cm long that have tiny pits (domatia) on the underside. Female plants carry dense clusters of orange berries. Small greenish wind-pollinated flowers in late winter–spring; orange berries in autumn on female plants.

In this photo: Female plant: dense clusters of oval berries ripening orange along the stems; leaves 6–12 cm, glossy, opposite, with tiny pits on the underside.

Photo: Peter de Lange (pjd1) (CC0 1.0).

practices.explanation: Large shrub or small tree with glossy, opposite, oblong leaves 6–12 cm long that have tiny pits (domatia) on the underside. Female plants carry dense clusters of orange berries.

media.alt: A stem crowded with clusters of glossy orange and green berries among long glossy leaves

items.context:
Taupata (looking-glass plant), Coprosma repens, is found only in New Zealand. Coastal shrub with thick, broad, extremely glossy dark-green leaves that look polished or wet. Leaves are broadly oval to round, often with a small notch at the tip. Small greenish flowers in spring; orange-red berries on female plants in summer–autumn.

In this photo: Dense coastal shrub with thick, extremely glossy leaves that look polished or wet.

Photo: Rudolph89 (CC0 1.0).

practices.explanation: Coastal shrub with thick, broad, extremely glossy dark-green leaves that look polished or wet. Leaves are broadly oval to round, often with a small notch at the tip.

media.alt: A dense mass of thick, very shiny bright green leaves on a coastal shrub

items.context:
Kōtukutuku (tree fuchsia), Fuchsia excorticata, is found only in New Zealand. The world's largest fuchsia: a small tree with orange-red papery bark peeling in thin strips, and thin leaves that are silvery-white underneath. It loses its leaves in winter in colder places. Hanging green-and-purple flowers that age to dark red, with striking blue pollen, often growing straight from the branches in late winter and spring; dark purple berries follow.

In this photo: Distinctive papery, red-brown to orange bark peeling in thin strips; the tree is deciduous in colder areas.

Photo: John Barkla (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: The world's largest fuchsia: a small tree with orange-red papery bark peeling in thin strips, and thin leaves that are silvery-white underneath. It loses its leaves in winter in colder places.

media.alt: A twisting trunk with orange-brown papery bark peeling off in thin sheets

items.context:
Toetoe, Austroderia toetoe, is found only in New Zealand. Large native tussock grass with long arching leaves and tall stems of drooping, feathery, cream to golden plumes. Unlike the weedy pampas grass, the plumes droop to one side, appear in spring–early summer, and the dead leaves do not curl into wood-shaving-like coils at the base. Plumes from about September to January depending on the species and altitude.

In this photo: Big clumping grass with long arching leaves and tall stems of cream-gold, drooping, feathery plumes in spring–summer.

Photo: Tim Park (CC BY-SA 4.0).

practices.explanation: Large native tussock grass with long arching leaves and tall stems of drooping, feathery, cream to golden plumes. Unlike the weedy pampas grass, the plumes droop to one side, appear in spring–early summer, and the dead leaves do not curl into wood-shaving-like coils at the base.

media.alt: Large tussocks of long arching grass topped by many drooping cream-gold plumes on a hillside

items.context:
Pīngao (golden sand sedge), Ficinia spiralis, is found only in New Zealand. Sand-dune sedge with stiff, curved leaves that turn golden-orange, forming loose tufts that creep through the sand. Easily told from introduced marram grass by its golden colour and dark brown, knobbly flower heads. Dark chocolate-brown flower and seed heads on stiff stems in spring and early summer.

In this photo: Golden-orange to yellow-green sedge forming loose tufts on sand dunes, with stiff, curved leaves.

Photo: Tomas Sobek (CC BY 2.0).

practices.explanation: Sand-dune sedge with stiff, curved leaves that turn golden-orange, forming loose tufts that creep through the sand. Easily told from introduced marram grass by its golden colour and dark brown, knobbly flower heads.

media.alt: A tufted clump of curving yellow-green and orange leaves with dark seed heads growing on a sandy beach

items.context:
Kiekie, Freycinetia banksii, is found only in New Zealand. Woody climber whose stems carry tufts of long, narrow, flax-like leaves, scrambling over the forest floor or climbing tree trunks. Flowers sit within fleshy white to lilac bracts, and fruits are fat, knobbly green cylinders. Flower heads with fleshy edible bracts August–November; fruits January–May.

In this photo: Woody climber whose stems carry tufts of long, narrow, flax-like leaves; scrambles over the ground or climbs tree trunks.

Photo: Hannah Rogers (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Woody climber whose stems carry tufts of long, narrow, flax-like leaves, scrambling over the forest floor or climbing tree trunks. Flowers sit within fleshy white to lilac bracts, and fruits are fat, knobbly green cylinders.

media.alt: A climbing plant with long narrow arching leaves in tufts, scrambling up a tree fern trunk

items.context:
Kareao (supplejack), Ripogonum scandens, is found only in New Zealand. Forest vine that forms tangled thickets of tough, smooth, dark cane-like stems that loop around trunks. Leaves are glossy with three main veins, and young shoot tips look like asparagus. Small greenish flowers in summer; bunches of bright red berries are present much of the year.

In this photo: Thickets of tough, leafless, dark brown stems looping and tangling between trees; leaves are mostly high up in the canopy.

Photo: Karora (Public domain).

practices.explanation: Forest vine that forms tangled thickets of tough, smooth, dark cane-like stems that loop around trunks. Leaves are glossy with three main veins, and young shoot tips look like asparagus.

media.alt: A dense, impenetrable tangle of thin dark woody stems criss-crossing through forest undergrowth

items.context:
Puawānanga (white clematis), Clematis paniculata, is found only in New Zealand. Climber that drapes forest edges and canopies with sprays of large, pure-white starry flowers in early spring. Leaves are glossy and divided into three leaflets. Large white flowers (5–10 cm) from about August to November, then fluffy seed heads.

In this photo: Climber draping over the forest canopy, covered in sprays of large white starry flowers in early spring.

Photo: tomsubritzky (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Climber that drapes forest edges and canopies with sprays of large, pure-white starry flowers in early spring. Leaves are glossy and divided into three leaflets.

media.alt: A vine smothering a bushy tree with many starry white flowers in spring

items.context:
Ngaio, Myoporum laetum, is found only in New Zealand. Coastal small tree with fleshy, bright green leaves densely dotted with translucent oil glands (hold one up to the light). Young leaves are sticky and toothed near the tip. Small white flowers spotted with purple, October–January; red-purple berries in late summer–autumn. All parts are poisonous to livestock.

Kāpuka (broadleaf), Griselinia littoralis, is found only in New Zealand. Hardy small tree, common in southern and mountain areas and as hedging, with thick, very glossy, apple-green oval leaves on yellowish stalks. Leaves are smooth-edged and often slightly unequal at the base. Inconspicuous tiny greenish flowers in spring; small dark purple berries on female plants.

Māhoe (whitey wood), Melicytus ramiflorus, is found only in New Zealand. Common small tree of regenerating bush with pale, whitish bark and thin, bright green, evenly toothed leaves. Clusters of tiny flowers and then violet-purple berries grow straight from the twigs below the leaves. Tiny yellowish flowers in summer; violet to purple berries on the twigs in summer–autumn.

In this photo: Small violet to purple berries crowded directly along the twigs below the leaves (summer–autumn).

Photo: paul-tebbutt (CC BY-NC 4.0).

Tawa, Beilschmiedia tawa, is found only in New Zealand. Tall forest tree of the North Island and top of the South with dark trunks and fine, drooping foliage of narrow, willow-like, pale-green leaves that are bluish underneath. Fruits are large and plum-like. Tiny flowers in spring–summer; dark purple, olive-shaped fruits (2–3 cm) ripen in late summer.

In this photo: Tall forest tree with dark trunks and fine, willow-like, drooping foliage of narrow pale-green leaves.

Hangehange, Geniostoma ligustrifolium, is found only in New Zealand. Understorey shrub of northern forests with soft, glossy, pale yellow-green, pointed leaves in opposite pairs. Clusters of tiny greenish-white starry flowers sit at the leaf joints. Small greenish-cream, scented flowers in spring, then small capsules.

In this photo: Bushy understorey shrub with light, yellowish-green, glossy, soft leaves in opposite pairs.

Photo: Bjankuloski06 (CC BY 4.0).

Rangiora (bushman's friend), Brachyglottis repanda, is found only in New Zealand. Big shrub with very large, soft, wavy-edged leaves that are green above and covered in white felt underneath. Leaves are poisonous if eaten. Large sprays of small, fragrant, creamy daisy flowers from late winter to spring.

In this photo: Big, spreading shrub with large, soft, wavy-margined leaves that look pale on the underside.

Photo: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz (CC BY-SA 4.0).

practices.explanation: Big shrub with very large, soft, wavy-edged leaves that are green above and covered in white felt underneath. Leaves are poisonous if eaten.

Kōwhai ngutukākā (kākābeak), Clianthus puniceus, is found only in New Zealand. Sprawling shrub with fern-like leaves of many small leaflets and drooping clusters of large scarlet flowers shaped like a kākā's beak. Almost extinct in the wild; usually met in gardens and restoration plantings. Red claw-shaped flowers mostly August–January; pods follow.

In this photo: Sprawling, soft-wooded shrub with fern-like pinnate leaves and drooping clusters of scarlet, beak-shaped flowers.

practices.explanation: Sprawling shrub with fern-like leaves of many small leaflets and drooping clusters of large scarlet flowers shaped like a kākā's beak. Almost extinct in the wild; usually met in gardens and restoration plantings.

Tawhai (silver beech), Lophozonia menziesii, is found only in New Zealand. Large beech of cool and mountain forests with small, rounded leaves (under 1.5 cm) edged with neat round teeth, held in flat sprays. Younger trunks have smooth silvery-white bark with horizontal markings. Small inconspicuous flowers in spring–early summer; heavy seeding only in mast years.

In this photo: Mossy, gnarled trunks with a canopy of tiny leaves forming dense, layered sprays; typical of high-rainfall mountain beech forest.

Photo: Jason Hollinger (CC BY 2.0).

practices.explanation: Large beech of cool and mountain forests with small, rounded leaves (under 1.5 cm) edged with neat round teeth, held in flat sprays. Younger trunks have smooth silvery-white bark with horizontal markings.

Mount Cook buttercup, Ranunculus lyallii, is found only in New Zealand. The world's largest buttercup, growing in wet subalpine and alpine areas. Huge, round, glossy, saucer-shaped leaves have the stalk attached in the middle, and large white flowers with yellow centres are held above them. White flowers 5–8 cm across from about October to January.

In this photo: Large alpine herb forming drifts in wet subalpine areas; huge round, saucer-shaped leaves and many white flowers held above them.

Photo: johnnoh (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: The world's largest buttercup, growing in wet subalpine and alpine areas. Huge, round, glossy, saucer-shaped leaves have the stalk attached in the middle, and large white flowers with yellow centres are held above them.

items.context:
Pōhutukawa (New Zealand Christmas tree), Metrosideros excelsa, is found only in New Zealand. Broad, spreading coastal tree, often on cliffs, with a gnarled trunk and hanging aerial roots. Leaves are thick and leathery with dense white felt underneath, and young shoots and buds are woolly. Masses of crimson brush-like flowers (bunches of long stamens) from late November to January; small woody seed capsules follow.

In this photo: Spreading rounded crown smothered in crimson brush-like flowers in early summer; short trunk branching low.

Photo: IdiotSavant (CC BY-SA 4.0).

practices.explanation: Broad, spreading coastal tree, often on cliffs, with a gnarled trunk and hanging aerial roots. Leaves are thick and leathery with dense white felt underneath, and young shoots and buds are woolly.

items.context:
Rātā (northern rātā), Metrosideros robusta, is found only in New Zealand. Huge forest tree that usually starts life as an epiphyte high on another tree, sending roots down that fuse into a massive, fluted, hollow trunk. Flowers look like pōhutukawa but the leaves are smaller, glossy and lack white felt underneath. Scarlet brush flowers in summer (mostly December–January), with heavy flowering in some years and sparse flowering in others.

In this photo: Scarlet stamen-brush flowers in clusters at branch tips; leaves small, thick and glossy without white felt underneath.

Photo: Ollie Gibson (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Huge forest tree that usually starts life as an epiphyte high on another tree, sending roots down that fuse into a massive, fluted, hollow trunk. Flowers look like pōhutukawa but the leaves are smaller, glossy and lack white felt underneath.

media.alt: Clusters of scarlet brush-like flowers among small dark green leaves

Kōwhai, Sophora microphylla, is found only in New Zealand. Small tree with feathery leaves made of many tiny paired leaflets, and drooping clusters of golden tubular flowers in late winter to spring. Several kōwhai species look alike; this one has a tangled, zigzag juvenile stage. Golden-yellow pea flowers (often before or with new leaves) from about August to October, followed by knobbly, beaded seed pods with hard yellow seeds.

In this photo: Juvenile (divaricating) form: interlaced zigzag stems with very few tiny leaflets, forming a springy tangle quite unlike the adult tree.

Photo: Jon Sullivan (CC BY 4.0).

practices.explanation: Small tree with feathery leaves made of many tiny paired leaflets, and drooping clusters of golden tubular flowers in late winter to spring. Several kōwhai species look alike; this one has a tangled, zigzag juvenile stage.

Harakeke (New Zealand flax), Phormium tenax, is found only in New Zealand. Large clump of stiff, tough, sword-shaped leaves up to 3 m long that fan from the base. Tall dark flower stalks rise well above the leaves; seed pods are short, stiff and point upward. Dull red tubular flowers on stalks up to 4–5 m from October to December, much visited by tūī; upright three-sided pods follow.

In this photo: Tall, dark, branched flower stalk well above the leaves; flowers dull red and tubular.

Photo: Simon Nicholas (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Large clump of stiff, tough, sword-shaped leaves up to 3 m long that fan from the base. Tall dark flower stalks rise well above the leaves; seed pods are short, stiff and point upward.

items.context:
Wharariki (mountain flax), Phormium cookianum, is found only in New Zealand. A smaller, softer flax than harakeke with thinner leaves that arch and droop. The surest cue is the seed pods: long, slender, twisted and hanging down. Greenish-yellow flowers in early summer, then long twisted pods that dangle from the flower stalk.

In this photo: Seed pods are long, thin and twisted and hang downward; the key difference from harakeke's short upright pods.

Photo: RuthP (CC BY-SA 2.0).

practices.explanation: A smaller, softer flax than harakeke with thinner leaves that arch and droop. The surest cue is the seed pods: long, slender, twisted and hanging down.

Tī kōuka (cabbage tree), Cordyline australis, is found only in New Zealand. Tree with a bare corky trunk that forks into branches, each ending in a dense pom-pom of long, narrow, grass-like leaves. Dead leaves hang as a skirt beneath each tuft. Huge sprays of tiny, sweet-scented creamy flowers in late spring (October–December), then small bluish-white berries.

In this photo: Huge branched sprays of small, sweet-scented cream flowers in late spring among the strap-like leaves.

Photo: Ruth Palsson (CC BY-SA 4.0).

practices.explanation: Tree with a bare corky trunk that forks into branches, each ending in a dense pom-pom of long, narrow, grass-like leaves. Dead leaves hang as a skirt beneath each tuft.

Ponga (silver fern), Alsophila dealbata, is found only in New Zealand. Tree fern whose mature fronds are bright silvery-white underneath. Old frond bases stay on the trunk as stubs rather than a full skirt of dead fronds. No flowers (spore-producing).

In this photo: Underside of mature fronds is a striking silvery white, the classic identifying feature.

Photo: lylescott (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: Tree fern whose mature fronds are bright silvery-white underneath. Old frond bases stay on the trunk as stubs rather than a full skirt of dead fronds.

media.alt: A fern frond showing a bright silvery-white underside against dark green fronds

Mamaku (black tree fern), Sphaeropteris medullaris, is native to New Zealand. New Zealand's tallest tree fern, with very long arching fronds on thick black stalks. Old fronds drop off cleanly, leaving a trunk patterned with oval or hexagonal scars, and the young koru are covered in black scales. No flowers (spore-producing).

In this photo: Huge koru (uncurling frond) and stalk covered in black, glossy scales; NZ's largest tree fern.

Photo: Tom Dale (CC BY-NC 4.0).

practices.explanation: New Zealand's tallest tree fern, with very long arching fronds on thick black stalks. Old fronds drop off cleanly, leaving a trunk patterned with oval or hexagonal scars, and the young koru are covered in black scales.

Wheki (rough tree fern), Dicksonia squarrosa, is found only in New Zealand. Slender, dark tree fern whose trunk bristles with the snapped-off bases of old frond stalks. Frond stalks are rough with dark brown hairs, and fronds are green on both sides; it often grows in clumps. No flowers (spore-producing).

In this photo: Frond stalks and midribs are rough with stiff dark brown hairs; leaflets green on both sides (not silver underneath).

Nīkau (nīkau palm), Rhopalostylis sapida, is found only in New Zealand. New Zealand's only native palm: a slender ringed grey trunk, a smooth bulging green crownshaft, and stiff, upswept feather-like fronds like a feather duster. Pinkish-lilac branched flower clusters burst from just below the crownshaft (summer–autumn), followed by slowly ripening bright red berries.

In this photo: Branched pink-lilac flower clusters burst from the trunk below the smooth green crownshaft; ringed trunk visible.

Kauri, Agathis australis, is found only in New Zealand. Giant conifer of northern forests with a massive, straight, branchless trunk of smooth grey bark that flakes in thick round scales, crowned high above the canopy. Leaves are thick, leathery and strap-shaped; cones are round balls. Round female cones (spring to autumn) break apart on the tree to release winged seeds; small cylindrical male cones occur on the same tree.

In this photo: Young 'ricker': slim conical shape with branches along the whole trunk, very different from the bare-trunked, flat-crowned mature tree.

Photo: Bjankuloski06 (CC BY 4.0).

Rimu (red pine), Dacrydium cupressinum, is found only in New Zealand. Tall forest conifer whose branchlets hang down in soft, drooping ropes of tiny, overlapping, scale-like needles. Bark peels in large, thick flakes. Small fruits: a black seed on a red fleshy cup, mostly February–May, and heavily only in mast years.

In this photo: Juvenile form: long pendulous ropes of soft, overlapping scale-like needles giving a weeping look; adults are much less droopy.

Photo: Petra Gloyn (CC BY-NC 4.0).

Trunk bases are buttressed and adult foliage is tiny, overlapping scales. Fruits ripen February–April: a blue-black seed sitting on a swollen orange-red fleshy base.

Adult leaves are short, flat, blunt needles in two rows, pale bluish underneath. Round, dark blue-black to plum-coloured fruits about 1 cm across with a waxy bloom; they take 12–18 months to ripen.

Leaves are broadly oval to round, often with a small notch at the tip. Small greenish flowers in spring; orange-red berries on female plants in summer–autumn.

In this photo: Leaves broad-oval with a rounded or notched tip, thick and so glossy they reflect light (hence 'looking-glass plant').

Kōtukutuku (tree fuchsia), Fuchsia excorticata, is found only in New Zealand. The world's largest fuchsia: a small tree with orange-red papery bark peeling in thin strips, and thin leaves that are silvery-white underneath. It loses its leaves in winter in colder places. Hanging green-and-purple flowers that age to dark red, with striking blue pollen, often growing straight from the branches in late winter and spring; dark purple berries follow.

In this photo: Drooping fuchsia flowers, green and purple maturing to dark red, with striking blue pollen; flowers grow straight from branches and trunks.

Toetoe, Austroderia toetoe, is found only in New Zealand. Large native tussock grass with long arching leaves and tall stems of drooping, feathery, cream to golden plumes. Unlike the weedy pampas grass, the plumes droop to one side, appear in spring–early summer, and the dead leaves do not curl into wood-shaving-like coils at the base. Plumes from about September to January depending on the species and altitude.

In this photo: Plumes hang to one side and are golden or creamy, not the stiff, upright, dense white heads of pampas grass.

Photo: metanature (CC BY 4.0).

Easily told from introduced marram grass by its golden colour and dark brown, knobbly flower heads. Dark chocolate-brown flower and seed heads on stiff stems in spring and early summer.

Dull red tubular flowers on stalks up to 4–5 m from October to December, much visited by tūī; upright three-sided pods follow.

Kauri, Agathis australis, is found only in New Zealand. Giant conifer of northern forests with a massive, straight, branchless trunk of smooth grey bark that flakes in thick round scales, crowned high above the canopy. Leaves are thick, leathery and strap-shaped; cones are round balls. Round female cones (spring to autumn) break apart on the tree to release winged seeds; small cylindrical male cones occur on the same tree.
